opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've spent a lot of time thinking about. The headline in our original paper was that the length of tasks models could complete at 50% reliability was doubling roughly every seven months, looking back over about six years. When you zoom in on the more recent models, from 2024 onward, the doubling time looks noticeably shorter, maybe closer to four months. So the question is whether that's a real change in the underlying trend or an artifact of how we're measuring.

I think the honest answer is that it's probably some of both, and we're uncertain about the mix.

On the "it's real" side, there are plausible mechanisms. The big shift in this period was reinforcement learning on agentic and reasoning tasks, training models to work through multi-step problems, use tools, recover from errors, and keep going rather than giving up or derailing. Many of the failures we saw in earlier models on longer tasks weren't about lacking knowledge. They were about getting stuck in loops, failing to notice a mistake, or not persisting. If training specifically targets those failure modes, you'd expect long-horizon performance to improve faster than general capability. So a kink in the curve around when labs started heavily investing in this kind of training isn't surprising.

On the measurement side, I want to be careful. Our task suite is finite, and at the longer end, the multi-hour tasks, we have relatively few tasks, so estimates there are noisier. The tasks are also mostly software engineering and research-flavored, and fairly well specified with clean automatic scoring. It's possible recent training is particularly well aligned with exactly that kind of task, so we're seeing faster progress in a domain that's especially amenable to it, and that might not generalize to messier real-world work. We've done some work looking at how "messiness" affects performance, and models do worse on messier tasks, though the trend over time seems broadly similar. Still, that's a real caveat.

There's also a fitting question. With a short window and few data points, whether you see a four-month or seven-month doubling depends on which models you include and where you draw the line. I wouldn't put a lot of weight on the precise number.

So my overall take: I think there's decent evidence that progress on these kinds of agentic tasks has sped up, and there's a sensible story for why. But I'd be cautious about extrapolating the faster rate far into the future, and cautious about assuming it maps one-to-one onto real-world usefulness. The thing I'd most want people to take away is that the trend has been robust enough across a lot of methodological choices that it's worth taking seriously, and the error bars are wide in both directions, which is itself important for forecasting.

r004.rationale: It mentions a possible four-month doubling rate from 2024 onward, but does not offer a low-confidence hypothesis that task horizons are now following an exponential trend at that rate.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few things going on, and I want to be careful to separate what we actually measured from the stories people tell about it.

The headline result from the original time horizons paper was this roughly seven-month doubling time over the 2019 to 2024 period. And then when you look at just the models from, say, late 2024 onward, the fit looks faster, something closer to four months. So the natural question is whether that's a real change in the underlying trend or whether it's an artifact of how we're measuring.

My honest take is that I don't think we can confidently say it's a real break in the trend yet. There are a couple of reasons for that. One is just that the number of data points on the post-2024 side is small. If you fit an exponential to a handful of models, you can get pretty wild estimates of the doubling time, and the confidence intervals are wide enough that the slower trend isn't ruled out. People see a steeper line on a log plot and update really hard, and I think that's a bit premature.

The second thing is that the task suite itself has limitations that matter more as the horizons get longer. The tasks at the top end of our distribution are things like multi-hour software engineering and research engineering tasks, and there just aren't that many of them. So the measurement at the long end is noisier. And these are also tasks that are, in some sense, well-specified and self-contained in ways that a lot of real-world work isn't. If labs are specifically optimizing for agentic coding, which they clearly are, you'd expect to see outsized gains on exactly this kind of benchmark relative to the broader economy.

That said, I don't want to be dismissive either. There are plausible mechanistic reasons you'd expect acceleration. The big one is that a lot of the recent progress is coming from reinforcement learning on agentic tasks, and that's a relatively new lever that labs are pulling hard. If you went from a regime where capabilities were mostly coming from pretraining scale to one where there's a new, cheap, fast-moving source of improvement, you'd expect the curve to bend upward for a while. Whether it keeps bending or saturates is the real question.

So where I land is something like: the acceleration is probably partly real and partly measurement. I'd put meaningful weight on the faster doubling time being right over the next year or two. But I'd also want to see a few more model releases, and ideally better coverage of really long tasks, before I'd say the trend has definitively shifted. And I'd push back on anyone who treats the four-month number as a settled fact and extrapolates it out five years.

astra-6.text:
I’d be cautious about interpreting it as a change in the underlying trend. The time horizon is the length of a task, measured by how long it takes a human, that an AI can complete at some specified success rate. So it’s not directly measuring how long an AI can operate autonomously, and it’s not a general measure of how quickly AI capabilities are improving.

An apparent acceleration could reflect faster underlying progress, but it could also reflect improvements that are particularly useful on the tasks in the benchmark, or sensitivity to which models and dates you include in the fit. With relatively few observations near the end of a time series, it can be hard to distinguish those explanations.

I’d want to see whether the faster trend persists across subsequent models, different task sets, and different success thresholds. I think it’s evidence worth taking seriously, but I wouldn’t confidently extrapolate a new, faster doubling rate from the apparent bend alone.

r003.rationale: It does not compare four- and seven-month doubling trends or state that the former predicted subsequent progress better.

r004.rationale: It declines to confidently extrapolate a faster doubling rate and does not propose, even with low confidence, a four-month exponential trend.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be cautious about interpreting it as a clear change in the underlying rate of progress. The time horizon is the duration of tasks that a model can complete at a given success rate, and estimating that involves choices about the tasks, the human baselines, and how you fit the trend. With relatively few model releases, the apparent slope can be quite sensitive to those choices.

But there’s a plausible substantive story, too: models are getting better at using tools, checking their work, and recovering from mistakes. Those improvements can make a big difference on longer tasks, where you have more opportunities to go off track. So I take the acceleration seriously as a possibility, but I wouldn’t confidently extrapolate that steeper trend from the post-2024 points alone.
